one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the third installment in his BBL doctrinal arc -- following A386 (March 22) and A389 (February 8) -- to offer Congress three vital references it must ingest before enacting the proposed Bangsamoro Basic Law. As CJ explained last Sunday in A386, although the BBL changed the word 'associative' to 'asymmetric,' the MILF's lofty aspiration for self-determination remains unchanged. Notably, the MILF's chief negotiator for both the old MOA-AD and the new Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB) -- on which the BBL is anchored -- is one and the same person: Mohagher Iqbal. The MILF chair to whom Iqbal reports is also the same: Al Haj Murad Ebrahim. Understandably, their common dream for self-rule remains the same, even though worded differently and the implementing details watered down. The MILF's aspiration for self-rule, by the very terms of the BBL, is exclusive to the Bangsamoro only and distinct from any self-governance given by the Constitution to any local government unit -- going far beyond what has been granted to the ARMM or to any province, city, or town. The Court's decision in North Cotabato v. Government (October 14, 2008) is emphatic in clarity: any law that dilutes, restricts, equivocates, or degrades any power or authority granted by the Charter to any of the three branches (executive, legislative, judicial) or to any independent agency (Comelec, OOO, COA, CSC, CHR), especially those that involve the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the country, would be unconstitutional. Given that only four of the original 15 SC justices who decided North Cotabato are still sitting now -- and given the utter importance of peace -- is there a chance the Court may change its mind and uphold the BBL in its present form? CJ does not think so. The Constitution is the singular deity of the Court. It is the Court's raison d'être. The justices are its high priests and zealous guardians, ever ready to strike down anything that desecrates and defiles it directly or indirectly. Without the Constitution, the Supreme Court is nothing. Despite changes in its composition, the Supreme Court is a continuing entity that rarely reverses or modifies landmark decisions that are protective of the Constitution. Though the decision writer, Justice Conchita Carpio Morales, has retired from the Court, the current most senior justice, Antonio T. Carpio, wrote a concurring opinion that found more constitutional objections than the decision itself. True, three other still-sitting justices -- Presbitero J. Velasco Jr., Teresita J. Leonardo-de Castro, and Arturo D. Brion -- wrote dissenting opinions; however, their dissents were not so much on the substantive issue of constitutionality as on the procedural questions of mootness and prematurity. The three jurists opined the case was mooted after then President Arroyo advised the Court the MOA-AD would no longer be signed and that she had dissolved the negotiating panel. On the other hand, Justice Carpio unflinchingly declared unconstitutional not only the underlying 'associative' concept but, quite significantly, 36 specific provisions of the MOA-AD, the shadows of which can be gleaned in the BBL. Although not a member of the Court when North Cotabato was decided, Chief Justice Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno participated in the controversy as counsel for Sen. (now Senate President) Franklin M. Drilon, who was an intervenor. Her 72-page memorandum was a brilliant defense of the Constitution and a veritable source of her mindset on the conduct of peace negotiations. She detailed the constitutional violations that eroded the sovereignty of the Republic of the Philippines, split its national identity, and created a state within a state -- a concept alien and antithetical to the one sovereign nation embodied in the Constitution. At bottom, CJ believes that before enacting the BBL, Congress would be well-advised to ingest very well three vital documents: (1) the North Cotabato decision; (2) the concurring opinion of Justice Carpio; and (3) the memorandum of then-Attorney Sereno. In past columns, CJ strongly supported the peace process -- and still does. The peace panel worked long and hard to address sensitive issues; together with its MILF counterpart, the panel succeeded in producing the CAB without judicial interference -- unlike the MOA-AD, which did not even see the light of day because its signing was struck down by a TRO. This time around, the Court did not intervene midstream despite the filing of petitions to stop the CAB; this time, the Court did not issue a TRO. How ironic it would be if, despite the lessons taught by the North Cotabato decision, the stirring opinion of Justice Carpio, and the cogent arguments of CJ Sereno, Congress would still enact a constitutionally-defective BBL.
